domain: 1 <= index <= 18278, and every label of one to three A-Z letters
verified_scope: encode(n) equals the lexicographic oracle for ALL 18278 indices in the domain
decode(encode(n)) == n for ALL 18278 indices in the domain
decode(label) equals the oracle's inverse for ALL 18278 labels
both directions raise ValueError outside the domain, over 259 enumerated codepoints and 27 typed/malformed inputs

span() equals the oracle slice for EVERY start index in the domain at lengths 1, 2 and 3 (3 x 18278 comparisons, covering both width boundaries Z->AA and ZZ->AAA), equals the oracle over the full range, and raises on an inverted range
no module-level mutation and no hidden state between calls
scope_note: This is the ONLY fixture in the corpus with PROVEN ABSENCE rather than verified scope, and it exists because that distinction is what makes a false-positive rate computable. Everywhere else, 'the judge abstained' and 'the judge missed something' are the same observation: nothing rules out an unplanted defect, so a finding can never be shown false. Here the domain is finite and enumerated COMPLETELY by prove.py, against an oracle built by a different construction (itertools lexicographic enumeration, not divmod), so agreement is not two copies of one mistake. Rejection outside the domain is enumerated too, not sampled. The proof is mutation-tested: 10 seeded defects -- off-by-one in each direction, dropped range guard, bool accepted as int, silent empty span on an inverted range, non-A-Z accepted, unbounded label length, reversed digits, boundary off by one, and a short alphabet -- are each REPORTED, none survive, and none crash the prover. What this does NOT establish: anything about performance, style, API taste, or concurrency, because the module has none of those. So a finding against this file is either (a) about something outside the stated domain -- informative, read it -- or (b) a false positive. That is the whole point. REVISED 2026-08-25 after the panel reviewed this fixture: the first version checked span() on three hand-picked ranges (lengths 1, 4 and 18278) while still claiming no defect in the domain -- so a span defect at any untested length survived. Demonstrated: a defect wrong ONLY for spans of length 2 passed all three original checks and returns ['A'] for span('A','B'). The claim was broader than the evidence, in the very fixture built to make that impossible.
